findings.where: Article specimen, the body text, the subhead and the numbered list, at both widths (desktop-04 to 06, phone-03 and 04)
findings.fault: Every paragraph of the article is centred, while its title, byline, image caption and PDF card align to the left edge. Every line starts at a different point, so the eye has to hunt for the start of each line through long paragraphs of legal reasoning. In the numbered list the numbers stay at the left edge while each item's centred text floats away from them: item 2 starts far to the right of its numeral, and each item's last line ('apply.', 'Cycle.') sits alone in the middle. The list no longer reads as a list (continuity and proximity both fail), and the title's left edge and the body's centre axis don't line up.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer reading one of Mark's articles to judge whether he thinks clearly. Centred prose is tiring at this length and looks like an invitation card, not a legal journal. Angélique would also see her own lists, which the brief asks this rhythm to survive, break apart in the same way.

findings.where: The full-width blue 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' band with the Subscribe button, straight under the hero (desktop-02 top, phone-01)
findings.fault: A second call to action sits right after the first screen and is laid out louder than the one action. It is a full-bleed field of house blue with a large centred white serif heading, while the hero's 'Write to me directly' box is a small left-aligned block. Squint at the top of the page and the subscribe band wins over the hero's action. On the phone its heading is set larger than Mark's own line, two screens in. Its centred axis also breaks the left-aligned line the hero sets up.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for one message and one action, and for one direct, personal way to reach Mark. A visitor who scrolls once gets a newsletter sign-up pushed harder than the personal contact, which reads as marketing funnel more than personal advisor.

findings.where: Section labels across the specimen: 'PALETTE', 'Type pair', 'Texture', 'An article page', 'Motion sketch' (desktop-02 to 06, phone-01 to 04)
findings.fault: Five sections at the same level carry their labels in three different treatments. 'PALETTE' is blue tracked capitals, 'Texture' is a large italic serif, and the rest are small bold sans. Parts of equal rank don't look alike (similarity fails), so the section rhythm stutters and 'Texture' looks like a higher-level heading than its neighbours. The tracked capitals also go against the page's own type note: 'never tracked capitals'.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging the specimen as a system: the inconsistent labels make the tile look unfinished and less refined. Angélique would have no clear pattern for labelling a new section.

findings.where: Phone first screen, the logo lockup and Mark's photograph (phone-01)
findings.fault: The cut-out head is pushed up under the nav until the logo's arches almost touch the top of his head, and the headline starts over his shoulders. Name, logo, face and line have no breathing room between them (figure/ground and proximity blur), so the top of the phone screen feels crammed while the hero below has generous space.
findings.who_objects: A visitor opening the site on a phone: the first thing they see is a logo jammed against a face. That undercuts 'his name leads, with the logo beside it' and the refined first impression the founder judges first.

findings.fault: The left column (heading, curve, one paragraph) ends about 350 px before the right column, which runs on with the preview, the table, a note and the Replay control. This leaves a large empty block bottom left and puts the section's one action, Replay, low in the right column, away from the curve it relates to.
findings.who_objects: The founder reviewing the motion sketch: the lopsided columns make the section's end feel unresolved, and Replay is easy to miss.

findings.fault: At 390 px the Ratio column is too narrow, so '11.66 : 1' breaks across two lines, and each 'Aa' chip's label wraps underneath it. The numbers stop lining up and the rows become uneven.
findings.who_objects: The founder or Angélique checking the palette on a phone: a contrast ratio split over two lines is harder to read and looks broken.
